newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Angry Zaireans block aid for Rwandan refugees.
newsitem.headline: Angry Zaireans block aid for Rwandan refugees.

text.p: Hundreds of angry Zaireans stopped aid workers from reaching camps for 80,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees on Friday and the U.N. refugee agency suspended its operations.
The demonstrators prevented an aid convoy from leaving a ferry over the Zaire river, attacked vehicles and threatened aid workers in a protest over the refugees and the aid they are receiving.
Witnesses said some aid workers were held for over an hour. Foreign journalists who crossed the Zaire river were attacked.
Demonstrators told Reuters the refugees should move deeper into the jungle away from Kisangani, Zaire's third city. They said they did not want Western aid workers crossing the river.

It was the latest in a series of setbacks for the U.N. refugee agency UNHCR, which delayed airlifting a first batch of refugee children out of Kisangani on Friday because rebel officials said they feared it could spread cholera in the area.
"We are going to give them (refugees) one week and then we will go up to camps to fight them," said Tony Manda, a trader.
"It is better if the refugees go back into the forest and be taken home from there. We don't want them coming through town."
"The Zairean population refuses to let the whites (aid officials) take food to the refugees because the refugees are killing local Zaireans," said Yenga Masomboye, a boat operator.
UNHCR temporarily suspended its operations and told other foreign aid workers not to visit the camps, saying it was seeking security guarantees from rebel officials in Kisangani.

A spokeswoman for the U.N. World Food Programme (WFP) said Zaireans had in the last three days attempted to loot food aid from two warehouses in Kisangani and a train ferrying supplies to the refugees and local Zaireans living near the two camps.
"At the moment we have reports both our warehouses in the city have problems and are possibly being looted," she said.
"We have been feeding both Zairean internally displaced and some members of the local population for months," she added.
UNHCR spokeswoman Pam O'Toole said demonstrators stopped a convoy with two international and four local UNHCR employees and other aid workers, hammered on their vehicles and blocked their way.
Tensions were whipped up by aggressive local radio broadcasts against the refugees and unconfirmed reports in town that refugees had killed a rebel or several local Zaireans.
Aid workers, who declined to be identified, said they suspected rebels were inciting trouble to prevent the U.N. airlift via Kisangani of an estimated 100,000 Rwandan refugees.
"We have taken a step back today. Last night we were optimistic because we thought we could persuade authorities to let us start the repatriation," said UNHCR spokesman Paul Stromberg.
"We have had a security incident, fuel was requisitioned, so we are back to dealing with things on a very basic level."

He said rebel authorities on Friday requisitioned 60,000 litres of aircraft fuel due to be used for the refugee airlift to the eastern Zairean border city of Goma. Rebel officials gave no explanation.
Stromberg said UNHCR still hoped that rebel authorities in Kisangani would allow the airlift to start on Saturday.

A total of 330 cholera cases and 19 cholera deaths have been registered amnong 50,000 refugees at Kasese camp, 29 km (17 miles) south of Kisangani. About 30,000 refugees are camped at another site and another 20,000 are scattered further south.
The refugees are the rump of more than two million Hutus who fled Rwanda in 1994 after the victory of Tutsi rebels in the civil war and the genocide of 800,000 Tutsis and Hutu moderates.
Most returned home late last year but about 300,000 are believed to be stranded in Zaire, with the largest concentration between Kisangani and Ubundu, 125 km (75 miles) to the south.

The refugees are in a very poor state after trekking about 600 km (375 miles) since last October through dense jungle where they survived on grubs and tree-bark. They marched westwards to flee Tutsi-dominated rebels, supported by Rwanda's government.
